questions.question: What are Spring bean scopes?
questions.title: Spring Bean Scopes Overview
questions.direct_answer: **Bean scope** defines how many instances of a bean Spring creates and how long each lives. The two core scopes are **singleton** (the default — one instance per ApplicationContext) and **prototype** (a new instance every time it's requested), plus three web scopes: **request**, **session**, and **application**. Crucially, singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know all five bean scopes and can explain when each is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning singleton and prototype, forgetting the three web scopes (request, session, application)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prototype-in-singleton problem and how Spring uses scoped proxies to inject web scopes into singletons

sections.title: Bean Scopes Control Instance Lifecycle
sections.content:
**Bean scope** determines how many instances of a bean the Spring container creates and how long those instances live.

Think of it like a factory's production policy: do you make one reusable product everyone shares (singleton), or manufacture a fresh one for each customer (prototype)? Spring offers five scopes. The first two work in any Spring app: **singleton** creates one shared instance per ApplicationContext, and **prototype** creates a new instance every time the bean is requested. The other three are **web-specific scopes** available only in Spring MVC or WebFlux: **request** scope creates one instance per HTTP request, **session** scope creates one instance per user session, and **application** scope creates one instance per ServletContext (shared across all users).

The boundary detail interviewers probe: **singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM**. Two contexts in the same JVM each get their own singleton. Choosing the right scope prevents thread-safety bugs, memory leaks, and data leaking between users.

blue|prototype|~New each request|getBean returns a new object|Spring won't destroy it|Stateful helpers
emerald|request / session|~Web scopes|One per HTTP request|One per user session|Need a web context

sections.title: Singleton vs Prototype at a Glance
sections.content:
| Aspect | Singleton | Prototype |
|---|---|---|
| Instances | One per ApplicationContext | A new one every request |
| Default? | Yes | No, opt in with @Scope("prototype") |
| Best for | Stateless services | Stateful, short-lived beans |
| Destruction callback | @PreDestroy runs on context close | @PreDestroy never runs |
| Thread safety | Must be kept stateless | Each use is isolated |

sections.title: Mutable state in a singleton - data bug
Keep the singleton stateless
Defining Bean Scopes in Spring
When to Use Each Scope
sections.content:
Use **singleton** (the default) for stateless service classes like controllers, services, and repositories that hold no user-specific data. This is about 95% of your beans.

Use **prototype** when a bean has mutable state that shouldn't be shared — for example, a PDF generator that builds a report step by step, or a command object that accumulates user input.

Use **request** scope for beans that hold data valid only for one HTTP request, like a cart being checked out or search filters.

Use **session** scope for user-specific data that persists across multiple requests, like shopping cart contents, user preferences, or authentication state.

Use **application** scope for global shared state across all users, like app-wide configuration or metrics — rare in practice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting web scopes exist**: Freshers often think Spring only has singleton and prototype, missing that request, session, and application scopes exist in web apps.
- **Using singleton for stateful beans**: Storing user-specific data (like current cart items) in a singleton bean causes one user to see another user's data because the instance is shared across all threads.
- **Not using a scoped proxy for web scopes**: Injecting a request or session scoped bean into a singleton without proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS fails because Spring can't put a short-lived bean into a long-lived one — you get a BeanCreationException at startup.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Singleton scope**: one shared instance per ApplicationContext, the default for all beans, must be stateless for thread safety
**Prototype scope**: a new instance created every time the bean is injected or retrieved via getBean(); Spring does not manage its destruction
**Request scope**: one instance per HTTP request, destroyed when the request completes, requires a web environment
**Session scope**: one instance per user HTTP session, lives until session timeout or invalidation, great for user-specific data like carts
**Application scope**: one instance per ServletContext, shared across all users and sessions, used for app-wide shared state
**Scoped proxies**: required when injecting shorter-lived scopes (request, session) into longer-lived beans (singleton) via the proxyMode attribute
**Thread safety**: singleton beans are shared across threads, so any mutable state must be avoided or carefully synchronized

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Bean scope controls how many instances Spring creates and how long they live. There are five scopes. Singleton is the default — Spring makes one instance per ApplicationContext and reuses it everywhere. It's what you use for services and repositories because they're stateless. Prototype scope creates a new instance every time you inject it or call getBean. You'd use this for something with mutable state, like a report generator that builds data step by step. Then there are three web scopes. Request scope gives you one instance per HTTP request — created when the request starts and destroyed when it finishes. Session scope is one instance per user session, perfect for a shopping cart that lives across multiple requests. Application scope is one instance per ServletContext, shared by everyone — that's rare, maybe for app-wide config. One tricky thing is you can't just inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton. You need proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS so Spring injects a proxy that delegates to the current request or session instance. If you don't, the app won't start. The key insight is that singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM, and singleton beans must be stateless because they're shared across threads. If you store user-specific data in a singleton, one user can see another user's data. That's when you reach for prototype or session scope instead.

questions.direct_answer: **Singleton** is the default scope: Spring creates exactly one instance per **ApplicationContext** and injects that same object everywhere. It's ideal for stateless beans like @Service and @Repository, which must avoid mutable fields to stay thread-safe. Remember that singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.

sections.title: Singleton Scope: One Shared Instance
sections.content:
**Singleton scope** is the default bean scope in Spring. When you annotate a class with @Service, @Repository, or @Component without specifying a scope, Spring creates exactly one instance of that bean per **ApplicationContext** and reuses it for every injection point.

Think of it like a shared tool in a workshop: instead of giving each worker their own hammer, everyone uses the same one from the toolbox. This is efficient because creating objects is expensive, and most service-layer beans don't need separate instances.

The critical boundary is the **ApplicationContext**, not the JVM: **singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM**. If you run two Spring Boot apps in the same JVM, each has its own ApplicationContext and thus its own singleton instances. Singleton beans must be **stateless** (no mutable instance fields) because they're shared across all threads handling concurrent requests. If you store request-specific data in instance variables, you get data corruption and security bugs.

sections.title: Mutable field in a singleton - thread bug
Stateless singleton - thread-safe
Singleton Bean in Action
When to Use Singleton Scope
sections.content:
Use singleton scope for **stateless service classes** — beans that perform operations without storing mutable state in instance variables. Examples: @Service classes that orchestrate business logic, @Repository classes that talk to databases, @RestController classes that handle HTTP requests, and @Component utilities like validators or formatters. These beans typically have dependencies injected via the constructor and use only local variables within methods. Local variables are allocated per method call on the call stack, so they're naturally thread-safe. Singleton is the right choice for about 95% of your beans because it's memory-efficient and Spring manages the lifecycle automatically.

Avoid singleton when you need to store request-specific or user-specific data — that's when you need prototype, request, or session scope instead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking singleton means one per JVM**: Freshers often say singleton creates one instance per JVM, but it's one per ApplicationContext. With a parent-child context hierarchy or multiple Spring apps in one JVM (like integration tests), you'll have multiple singleton instances.
- **Storing mutable state in instance variables**: Adding a field like private String currentUser to a singleton service causes thread-safety bugs. Thread A sets it to Alice, then Thread B sets it to Bob before Thread A's request finishes — now Thread A sees Bob's data.
- **Expecting singleton state to survive restarts**: Singleton instances are created when the ApplicationContext starts and destroyed on shutdown. They're not persisted, so state is lost between application restarts.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Default scope**: every bean is singleton unless you specify a different scope via the @Scope annotation
**One per ApplicationContext**: the singleton boundary is the Spring container, not the JVM or classloader
**Shared across threads**: in a web app, the same singleton instance handles requests from multiple threads concurrently
**Stateless requirement**: singleton beans must not store mutable request-specific or user-specific data in instance fields
**Thread-safe by design**: use only final fields injected via constructor and local variables within methods
**Lifecycle management**: Spring calls @PostConstruct after construction and @PreDestroy before shutdown, each once per singleton
**Memory efficient**: reusing one instance across thousands of requests saves memory and avoids garbage collection overhead

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Singleton is the default scope in Spring. It means Spring creates exactly one instance of the bean per ApplicationContext and reuses that same instance everywhere it's injected. So if you have an OrderService annotated with at-Service, Spring creates one OrderService object when the context starts, and every controller or other service that needs it gets that same instance. It's important to know the boundary is the ApplicationContext, not the JVM. If you run two Spring apps in the same JVM, each has its own ApplicationContext, so you'd actually have two OrderService instances — one per app. The big reason singleton is the default is efficiency. Creating objects is expensive, and most beans don't need separate instances. But there's a critical rule: singleton beans must be stateless. That means no mutable instance fields storing request-specific data. In a web app, the same singleton instance handles requests from multiple threads at the same time. If you put something like private String currentUser as a field, Thread A sets it to Alice, then Thread B sets it to Bob before Thread A finishes — now Thread A sees Bob's data. That's a security bug. The safe pattern is to use only final fields injected via constructor, and keep request-specific data in local variables within methods. Local variables live on the stack, so each thread has its own copy automatically.

sections.title: Why Singleton is Spring's Default Bean Scope
sections.content:
**Singleton scope** means Spring creates exactly one instance of the bean per container and shares it across all injection points. It's the default because typical Spring applications follow a **stateless service architecture**: your service layer, repository layer, and controllers don't hold per-request data in instance fields.

They're just collections of methods that operate on parameters and return results. Think of a calculator — you don't need a separate one for each math problem because it doesn't remember previous calculations. A **UserService** with methods like findById or updateEmail is stateless: it doesn't store which user it's currently processing. Since these beans are stateless, sharing one instance is perfectly thread-safe.

Spring runs in **servlet containers** where hundreds of concurrent HTTP requests may execute simultaneously. If Spring defaulted to prototype, it would create hundreds of UserService instances all doing the same job, wasting heap and adding GC pressure. Singleton gives you **performance**, **memory efficiency**, and **simplicity**. And remember, singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.

sections.content:
amber|The Default|~singleton scope|One instance per context|Used if you set nothing|Shared everywhere
blue|Why Singleton|~Performance|Create once, reuse|Less GC pressure|Fits stateless services
emerald|Safe Because|~Services are stateless|No mutable fields|Logic uses params and locals|Thread-safe by design
rose|Watch Out|~If you add state|Shared across threads|Race conditions|Change scope or remove state

sections.title: Request data in a singleton field - race bug
Pass per-request data as parameters
Singleton Bean Shared Across Multiple Consumers
When Singleton Scope is Appropriate
sections.content:
Use singleton scope (the default) for any **stateless bean**: services, repositories, controllers, validators, mappers, utilities. A bean is stateless if it doesn't store per-request or per-user data in instance fields. For example, a PaymentService that calls external APIs is stateless even though it has a WebClient field — that field is the same for all requests, not request-specific data. Configuration beans like DataSource or RestTemplate are perfect singletons: you want one shared connection pool, not hundreds. **ThreadLocal** patterns also work with singleton — each thread gets its own copy even though the bean instance is shared.

Avoid singleton only when you need **per-request state** (use request scope), **per-session state** (use session scope), or **per-operation mutable state** (use prototype).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Storing request data in singleton fields**: Freshers add instance fields like private String currentUserId to a singleton service and update them during request processing. Concurrent requests overwrite each other's data. Pass request-specific data as method parameters.
- **Thinking singleton means single-threaded**: Singleton doesn't mean only one thread uses the bean at a time. Hundreds of threads can call methods on the same instance concurrently, so any mutable shared state causes race conditions. Singleton plus stateless equals thread-safe.
- **Using prototype without reason**: Some freshers mark beans prototype thinking it's safer, but prototype creates a new instance per injection (not per method call), increases memory use, and is usually wrong unless the bean holds mutable per-use state.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Singleton scope**: one instance per Spring container, created once and shared across all injection points and requests
**Stateless services**: most Spring beans hold no mutable instance fields, making singleton safe and efficient
**Thread safety**: singleton beans are accessed by multiple threads concurrently — statelessness prevents race conditions
**Memory efficiency**: one instance instead of thousands reduces heap usage and GC pressure in high-traffic apps
**Performance**: singleton avoids repeated instantiation and injection overhead for every request
**Design philosophy**: Spring promotes service-oriented design where logic lives in stateless methods, not object state
**When to use prototype**: only when you need mutable per-use state, like builders or accumulators

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The default scope is singleton because most beans in a Spring application are stateless services, and sharing one instance is both safe and efficient. A typical Spring app has services, repositories, and controllers that don't store any per-request data in instance fields. They just have methods that take parameters and return results. Since these beans don't hold state, there's no problem with multiple threads using the same instance concurrently — it's completely thread-safe. If Spring defaulted to prototype scope instead, it would create a new service instance for every injection point. Imagine having hundreds of UserService instances when one can serve the entire application. That's a huge waste of memory and CPU cycles. Spring runs in servlet containers where you might have hundreds of HTTP requests executing at the same time, all calling methods on the same singleton beans. This is fine because the beans are stateless. The singleton pattern gives you memory efficiency, better performance, and simpler lifecycle management. You'd only use a different scope like prototype or request when you need per-use mutable state or per-request data, which is rare. The vast majority of beans you write should be singleton because that's what the stateless service architecture is all about.

questions.question: What is the prototype bean scope and when do you use it?
questions.title: Spring Prototype Bean Scope
questions.direct_answer: **Prototype** scope makes Spring create a **new instance every time** the bean is injected or fetched via getBean(). Use it for **stateful** beans whose data must not be shared, like builders or command objects. Note that Spring does not call @PreDestroy on prototype beans — you clean them up yourself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when singleton scope is inappropriate and prototype is necessary
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Spring doesn't manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans — no @PreDestroy callback runs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prototype-in-singleton trap and all three fixes: ObjectProvider, @Lookup method injection, and ApplicationContext.getBean()

sections.title: Prototype Scope: Fresh Instance Every Time
sections.content:
**Prototype scope** tells Spring to create a new bean instance every single time the bean is injected or retrieved via ApplicationContext.getBean(). Unlike singleton (one shared instance), prototype is like ordering a custom-made sandwich — you get a fresh one each time. This is essential for **stateful beans** that accumulate data during their lifetime, like a PDF report generator that builds content step by step, or a command object that collects user input across method calls.

The key difference: Spring hands you the instance and then forgets about it. Spring does NOT manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans, so **@PreDestroy methods are never called** (whereas for a singleton @PreDestroy runs on context close). You're responsible for cleanup.

Prototype solves the thread-safety problem for stateful objects, but introduces the **prototype-in-singleton trap**: if you inject a prototype bean into a singleton via constructor, you only get one instance (created at singleton construction), defeating the purpose.

sections.title: Prototype Scope at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Is|~New bean each time|Per getBean or injection|Never cached|Good for stateful objects
blue|Lifecycle Gap|~Spring steps back|Creates and wires it|No destroy callback|You manage cleanup
emerald|When to Use|~Stateful, short-lived|Per-request builders|Command objects|Non-thread-safe helpers
rose|The Classic Trap|~Inside a singleton|Injected once equals one instance|Use @Lookup or ObjectProvider|Or a scoped proxy

sections.title: Prototype injected directly - acts like a singleton
ObjectProvider gives a fresh prototype
Defining a Prototype Bean
When to Use Prototype Scope
sections.content:
Use prototype scope when you need **stateful beans** where each usage requires isolated mutable state. Examples: a report generator that accumulates data before rendering, a shopping cart being built up during checkout, a multi-step wizard that collects user input across pages, or a command object that validates and processes form data. Prototype is also useful for **beans with different configurations per usage** — imagine a file processor that needs different output formats (PDF, CSV, JSON) configured per request.

The key signal you need prototype: if reusing the bean instance would let one operation see data from a previous operation, or if two concurrent operations would corrupt each other's state.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Injecting prototype into singleton via constructor**: The most common mistake. Spring creates one prototype instance at startup and reuses it forever — you lose prototype behavior. Use ObjectProvider, @Lookup method injection, or getBean() to get a fresh instance each time.
- **Expecting Spring to call @PreDestroy**: Spring doesn't track prototype beans after creation, so @PreDestroy methods never run. If your prototype holds resources like file handles or connections, close them manually.
- **Using prototype when you need request or session scope**: Freshers sometimes use prototype for web-scoped data like user sessions. That's wrong — you'll get a new instance on every injection, not one per request or session.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **New instance every time**: Spring creates a fresh bean on every getBean() call or every injection point
**Stateful beans**: prototype is designed for beans with mutable state that shouldn't be shared across uses
**No destruction lifecycle**: Spring does not call @PreDestroy on prototype beans — you must clean up resources
**Prototype-in-singleton trap**: injecting a prototype into a singleton via constructor gives you only one instance
**ObjectProvider fix**: inject ObjectProvider<YourBean>, then call getObject() for a fresh prototype each time
**@Lookup method injection**: annotate an abstract method with @Lookup; Spring returns a new instance on every call
**ApplicationContext.getBean()**: directly retrieve a new prototype, though it couples your code to Spring APIs

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Prototype scope means Spring creates a brand new instance every time you ask for the bean. If you inject it five times or call getBean five times, you get five separate objects. You'd use this when your bean has mutable state that shouldn't be shared. For example, imagine an invoice generator that accumulates line items and totals as you add products. If that's a singleton, multiple threads would corrupt each other's invoices. Making it prototype solves that — each invoice generation gets its own isolated instance. There's an important gotcha though. Spring doesn't manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans. If you have a at-PreDestroy method, it's never called. So if your prototype bean opens a file or database connection, you have to close it yourself. The other big trap is the prototype-in-singleton problem. If you inject a prototype bean into a singleton via constructor, you only get one instance created at startup, and that defeats the whole point. The fix is to use ObjectProvider. Instead of injecting the prototype directly, you inject ObjectProvider of that bean type, then call provider dot getObject inside your method to get a fresh instance every time. Another option is at-Lookup method injection, where you declare an abstract method and Spring returns a new instance on each call. The key thing to remember is prototype is for stateful beans where sharing an instance would cause bugs.

questions.question: What are request and session scopes in Spring?
questions.title: Request and Session Scopes in Spring
questions.direct_answer: **Request** scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request, destroyed when the response is sent. **Session** scope creates one instance per HTTP session, living until the session ends. Both are web-only and need **proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS** when injected into a singleton.

sections.title: Web Scopes for HTTP Request and Session Data
sections.content:
**Request scope** and **session scope** are web-specific bean scopes available only in Spring MVC or WebFlux applications. Request scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request — instantiated when the request starts and destroyed when the response is sent.

Think of it like a notepad you use during one phone call and throw away afterwards. **Session scope** creates one bean instance per user HTTP session — living from the user's first request (when the session is created) until session timeout or logout. It's like a file folder you keep for each customer with their preferences and history.

These scopes let you store temporary user-specific data without making your singleton services stateful. The critical detail: when you inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton, Spring can't directly inject the short-lived bean into the long-lived one. You must add **proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS** to the scope annotation. Spring then injects a proxy that delegates to the current request or session instance at runtime.

sections.title: Request vs Session Scope
sections.content:
amber|request scope|~One per HTTP request|New for each request|Dies when request ends|Holds per-call data
blue|session scope|~One per user session|Spans many requests|Dies on session end|Holds per-user data
emerald|Requirement|~Web context only|Needs a web app|Fails in a plain context|Use a scoped proxy to inject
violet|Inject Into Singleton|~proxyMode needed|TARGET_CLASS proxy|Resolves the real bean per request|Else stale data

sections.title: Request vs Session Scope
sections.content:
| Aspect | Request Scope | Session Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifecycle | Created per HTTP request, destroyed when response sent | Created per user session, destroyed on timeout or logout |
| Typical use case | Search filters, form data, request-specific context | Shopping cart, user preferences, authentication state |
| Annotation | @RequestScope or @Scope(WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST) | @SessionScope or @Scope(WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_SESSION) |
| Shared across requests | No, each request gets its own instance | Yes, the same instance across all requests in one session |
| Memory footprint | Low, destroyed quickly after each request | Higher, lives until the session expires (often 30 minutes idle) |

sections.title: Request bean injected directly - stale data
Scoped proxy resolves per request
When to Use Request and Session Scopes
sections.content:
Use **request scope** for data valid only for the duration of one HTTP request. Examples: user search filters, a temporary cart being checked out, request-specific audit context (user ID, correlation ID, IP address), or form submission data validated and processed in one request. Request scope keeps this data isolated so concurrent requests don't interfere.

Use **session scope** for user-specific data that persists across multiple requests. Examples: shopping cart contents built up over several pages, user preferences like language or theme, wizard state for multi-step forms, or authentication principal information. Session scope is cheaper than hitting a database or cache for every request, but watch memory — sessions can live 30 minutes after the last request.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting proxyMode when injecting into singletons**: The most common error. Without proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS, Spring throws a BeanCreationException at startup because it can't inject a shorter-lived bean into a longer-lived one. The proxy delays resolution until runtime.
- **Using session scope for data that belongs in the database**: Freshers store things like order history in session scope. Sessions expire, servers restart, and in a load-balanced setup session data might not replicate. Persistent data belongs in the database.
- **Not invalidating sessions on logout**: Session scoped beans live until you call HttpSession.invalidate(). If you don't, the old session can be hijacked or waste memory.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Request scope lifecycle**: instance created when the HTTP request starts, destroyed when the response is sent, one per concurrent request
**Session scope lifecycle**: instance created on first access in a session, destroyed on timeout or invalidate(), shared across that user's requests
**proxyMode requirement**: use proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS (or INTERFACES) when injecting request or session beans into singletons
**Scoped proxy mechanism**: Spring injects a CGLIB proxy that delegates to the actual request or session instance based on the current thread
**Thread safety**: request and session beans are naturally thread-safe because each request or session has its own instance
**Realistic session example**: a shopping cart stores items added across multiple pages and is cleared on checkout or logout
**Memory considerations**: session beans consume memory until session expiration, so avoid storing large objects

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Request and session scopes are web-specific scopes for storing HTTP-related data. Request scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request. It's born when the request comes in and destroyed when the response goes out. You'd use this for things like search filters or form data that's only relevant for one request. Session scope creates one instance per user session — it lives from the user's first request until they log out or the session times out, usually 30 minutes of inactivity. Session scope is perfect for a shopping cart. The user adds items across multiple requests as they browse, and the cart instance holds all those items until checkout. The tricky part is you can't just inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton service. Spring would complain at startup because you're putting a short-lived bean into a long-lived one. The fix is to add proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS to the scope annotation. That tells Spring to inject a proxy instead of the real bean. The proxy looks like the bean but delegates method calls to the actual request or session instance at runtime. So when your singleton service calls a method on the cart, the proxy figures out which session the current request belongs to and forwards the call to that session's cart. Without the proxy, you'd get a BeanCreationException. One pitfall is don't store things in session scope that belong in a database, like order history. Sessions expire and servers restart, so you'd lose that data.

beats.text: Request scope gives one bean per HTTP request. Session scope gives one per user session. Both differ from singleton, and singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.

Pick request scope for data that lives inside one request and flows through your layers. Pick session scope for user state that must survive several requests, like a multi-step checkout. Skip session scope in stateless JWT APIs, since there's no server session to hold.
The gotcha is both scopes need proxyMode TARGET_CLASS when you inject them into a singleton. Without it the singleton grabs one instance at startup and always serves the wrong request's data.

questions.question: What is the problem with injecting a prototype bean into a singleton in Spring?
questions.title: Prototype Bean in Singleton Problem
questions.direct_answer: When a **prototype** bean is injected into a **singleton** via constructor or field, Spring resolves it **only once** — at singleton creation — so the singleton reuses that single instance forever, silently defeating prototype scope. Fix it with **ObjectProvider**, **@Lookup** method injection, or a scoped proxy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Spring resolves dependencies at container startup and the lifecycle interaction between bean scopes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Spring creates a new prototype instance each time the singleton uses it, when injection happens only once at singleton creation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate all three fixes: ObjectProvider for lazy lookup, @Lookup method injection, and scoped proxies via proxyMode

sections.title: The Prototype-in-Singleton Injection Problem
sections.content:
Spring's **dependency injection** happens at bean creation time, not at method invocation time. When you inject a **prototype bean** into a **singleton bean**, Spring resolves that dependency once — when it creates the singleton during application startup. The singleton stores a reference to that single prototype instance and reuses it forever.

Think of it like a vending machine (singleton) that's supposed to dispense a fresh cup (prototype) each time, but it was built with one permanent cup attached. Every customer gets the same cup. The prototype loses its per-use semantics and effectively becomes a singleton.

This is a problem when the prototype holds **stateful data** like user-specific or per-request context. If UserSession is prototype-scoped but injected into a singleton OrderService, all users would share the same UserSession instance — a serious bug. The root cause is Spring's **eager dependency resolution**: it wires all dependencies when the container starts, not when your code calls a method. (And remember, singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.)

sections.title: Prototype-in-Singleton at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|The Problem|~Injection happens once|Singleton built one time|Prototype injected once|Same instance reused
amber|Why It Surprises|~You expect new each call|But the field is fixed|Scope ignored after wiring|A silent bug
blue|Fix 1: ObjectProvider|~Ask per use|provider.getObject()|Fresh prototype each call|Clean and typed
emerald|Fix 2: @Lookup|~Method injection|Spring overrides the method|Returns a new bean|Or use a scoped proxy

sections.title: Prototype @Autowired into a singleton
Fetch a fresh prototype via ObjectProvider
Prototype Bean and the @Lookup Alternative
When This Problem Occurs
sections.content:
This issue appears when you mix **stateful prototype beans** with **singleton services**. Common scenarios: (1) a prototype holding per-request user context injected into a singleton REST controller — every request sees the same context. (2) a prototype with per-operation metrics injected into a singleton service — metrics from different operations get mixed. (3) a prototype builder with mutable state cached in a singleton — concurrent threads corrupt each other's state.

The problem doesn't occur if the prototype is truly stateless — but then you should just use singleton scope. Use ObjectProvider, @Lookup method injection, or scoped proxies whenever you need fresh prototype instances from a singleton.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting magic prototype behavior**: Freshers assume marking a bean prototype makes Spring create new instances whenever it's used, even after injection. Spring only honors prototype at injection time — inject once into a singleton and you get one instance forever.
- **Using ApplicationContext.getBean() everywhere**: Some freshers scatter context.getBean(PrototypeBean.class) through their code, turning Spring into a service-locator anti-pattern. Use ObjectProvider — it's type-safe and built for this.
- **Marking beans prototype without justification**: If your bean has no mutable state, singleton is better. Prototype is only for beans that hold per-use state that can't be shared.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Injection time**: Spring resolves dependencies when creating the singleton, not when methods are called — the prototype is instantiated once
**Scope mismatch**: a longer-lived scope holding a shorter-lived one promotes the shorter scope to the longer scope's lifetime
**ObjectProvider<T>**: the recommended fix — call getObject() each time you need a fresh prototype
**@Lookup method injection**: annotate an abstract method returning the prototype; Spring returns a new instance per call
**Scoped proxy**: use @Scope(value="prototype", proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) to inject a delegating proxy
**Stateless beans use singleton**: if your prototype has no mutable fields, just use the default singleton
**Thread safety**: prototype beans with state are safe per use but lose that safety when stuck in a singleton

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The problem is that Spring injects dependencies when it creates the singleton bean, not when you call methods on it. So if you inject a prototype bean into a singleton using constructor or field injection, Spring creates that prototype instance once during application startup. The singleton holds onto that single instance forever, effectively making the prototype behave like a singleton. Let's say you have a RequestProcessor that's prototype-scoped because it holds request-specific data like a request ID. If you inject it directly into a singleton OrderService, every order processed by that service uses the same RequestProcessor with the same request ID. That defeats the whole purpose. The cleanest fix is ObjectProvider. Instead of injecting RequestProcessor directly, you inject ObjectProvider of RequestProcessor, then in your method you call provider dot getObject to get a fresh instance each time. Spring also supports at-Lookup method injection where you define an abstract method that returns the prototype, and Spring implements it to return new instances. You can also use scoped proxies by setting proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS in the at-Scope annotation, which makes Spring inject a proxy that delegates to fresh instances. The key thing to remember is that prototype scope only works at injection time — once injected, it's just a regular object reference.

beats.text: The prototype-in-singleton problem happens when you wire a prototype bean straight into a singleton. Spring injects it once at startup, and the singleton holds that one instance for life. And singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.
Spring wires dependencies once, at startup. The singleton asks for a processor, Spring injects one prototype, and that's it. Nothing re-injects the field on later calls unless you design for it.

items: Wrong pattern: @Autowired processor in a singleton gives one instance for life.
ObjectProvider fix: inject ObjectProvider and call getObject for a fresh one.
@Lookup fix: Spring overrides an abstract method to return a new prototype each call.
getBean fix works but it's the service locator anti-pattern, so avoid it.

beats.text: Say TaskService is a @Service singleton and TaskProcessor is @Scope prototype with per-task state. Wire the processor in directly and every task shares it, so state from one bleeds into the next. Here's the non-obvious part. Injecting an ObjectProvider and calling getObject gives each task its own fresh processor.

items: The bug is silent. Spring never warns that the prototype degraded to singleton behavior.
Don't reach for getBean in your service layer. It's the service locator anti-pattern and hurts testing.

speakable_v2.cap: Wiring a prototype straight into a singleton silently breaks it. Use ObjectProvider or @Lookup for a fresh instance.
